course: Embedded Electronic Engineering A – Real-Time Systems

entries.objective:
Establish a structured work plan for Milestone 2 (M2) of the Real-Time
Systems seminar assignment on the Priority Exchange server algorithm.
The objective is to identify the sub-sections that M2 must cover
according to the assignment specification by Prof. Dr. Henkler,
allocate them across the available preparation days, and define
concrete deliverables for each working session. The output of this
interaction is intended to serve as the planning artefact that
organises the subsequent contextualisation and tradeoff analysis
phase of the seminar work.
entries.prompt:
Now tell me about M2: what sub-sectors will you categorise it into
to go through one by one? Instruct me one by one.
entries.ai_output_summary:
Provided a structured plan for Milestone 2 organised around six
sub-sections that correspond to the expected output as specified
by Prof. Dr. Henkler:

1. Related Approaches and Paradigms — mapping the lineage of
   aperiodic server algorithms from background scheduling through
   Polling Server, Deferrable Server, Priority Exchange, Sporadic
   Server, Dynamic Sporadic Server, Total Bandwidth Server, and
   Constant Bandwidth Server, establishing the position of
   Priority Exchange within this genealogy.
2. Competing Solution Strategies — non-server alternatives for
   aperiodic task handling, including Slack Stealing
   (Lehoczky and Ramos-Thuel, 1992), Dual-Priority Scheduling
   (Davis and Wellings, 1995), Earliest Deadline First-based
   servers, and modern resource reservation frameworks.
3. Assumptions Across Approaches — comparison of the task model,
   underlying scheduler, platform model, worst-case execution
   time knowledge, and resource-sharing handling assumed by each
   algorithm.
4. Tradeoff Analysis — application of the five tradeoff axes
   articulated in the assignment specification (precision versus
   runtime overhead, response time versus schedulability,
   optimality versus feasibility, offline versus online,
   formal guarantees versus practical deployability) to Priority
   Exchange and the comparable algorithms.
5. Consequences for Real-Time and Embedded Systems — practical
   deployment implications of selecting Priority Exchange versus
   Sporadic Server or Constant Bandwidth Server in production
   real-time operating systems, with reference to embedded
   constraints and certification standards (ISO 26262, DO-178C).
6. Scope and Boundaries of Related Work — explicit acknowledgment
   that Priority Exchange was introduced alongside Sporadic
   Server in a single 1989 paper, that modern citations are
   primarily of successors rather than competitors, and that
   the related-work landscape is therefore intentionally compact.

A day-by-day plan was provided allocating the six sub-sections
across the available working days from 26 May to 01 June 2026,
with concrete deliverables, suggested reading material, and
follow-up commands for each day. A target citation count of eight
to twelve well-chosen references was recommended, with an
indicative list including Sprunt, Sha and Lehoczky 1989, Buttazzo
"Hard Real-Time Computing Systems", Liu and Layland 1973,
Lehoczky, Sha and Strosnider 1987, Lehoczky and Ramos-Thuel 1992,
Davis and Wellings 1995, Spuri and Buttazzo 1996, and the course
slides of Prof. Dr. Henkler. A skeleton LaTeX document structure
based on the IEEEtran conference class was also provided to
facilitate direct integration with the M1 deliverable.

actions: The proposed sub-section structure was cross-checked against the
expected-output description in the assignment specification by
Prof. Dr. Henkler, which explicitly requires identification of
related approaches, neighbouring problem classes, design
alternatives, assumptions, and consequences. The principle of
avoiding artificial accumulation of weakly related references,
also stated in the assignment specification, is reflected in
the target citation count and in the explicit acknowledgment
that Priority Exchange's related-work landscape is compact.
The genealogy of aperiodic server algorithms (Polling Server,
Deferrable Server, Priority Exchange, Sporadic Server, Dynamic
Sporadic Server, Total Bandwidth Server, Constant Bandwidth
Server) and the attribution of the non-server alternatives
(Slack Stealing, Dual-Priority Scheduling) match the standard
treatment in the real-time scheduling literature, in particular
Buttazzo "Hard Real-Time Computing Systems".

issues: - The day-by-day allocation is a planning suggestion and not
derived from the assignment specification itself; it should
be adjusted to reflect the student's actual availability and
the progress made on each sub-section.
- Bibliographic references for the suggested citations are given
by author and year only; full bibliographic detail (venue,
pages, DOI) must be verified independently before inclusion
in the M2 deliverable.
- The recommendation of eight to twelve references is indicative
rather than prescribed by the assignment specification; the
appropriate number depends on the depth required for the
tradeoff analysis and on the related-work density of the
Priority Exchange topic.
- The LaTeX skeleton uses the IEEEtran conference class as in
Milestone 1; the assignment specification does not mandate
this class and an alternative template may be required if
specified by the seminar guidelines.
- The five tradeoff axes are taken from the assignment
specification but the mapping of Priority Exchange to each
axis is a preliminary characterisation and must be supported
by primary-source evidence in the final deliverable.
- The reference to ISO 26262 and DO-178C in the consequences
section is illustrative; their actual relevance to the
deployment of Priority Exchange should be verified against
the certification standards themselves before being asserted
in the M2 deliverable.
- The plan does not include an explicit phase for incorporating
feedback from the mentor on the M1 submission, which may
require revision of the contextualisation in M2.

entries.reflection:
The interaction produced a structured planning artefact for
Milestone 2 of the seminar assignment on the Priority Exchange
server algorithm. The six sub-sections identified — related
approaches and paradigms, competing solution strategies,
assumptions across approaches, tradeoff analysis, consequences
for real-time and embedded systems, and scope and boundaries of
related work — correspond directly to the expected-output
description in the assignment specification by Prof. Dr. Henkler
and provide a coherent organisational framework for the
contextualisation phase of the work.

The key methodological insight from this interaction is that the
Priority Exchange topic does not require an exhaustive accumulation
of related references but rather a focused mapping of the
algorithm's position within a tightly delimited family of
aperiodic server algorithms introduced primarily by Sprunt, Sha
and Lehoczky in 1989. The related-work landscape is therefore
characterised by its successors (Sporadic Server, Constant
Bandwidth Server) rather than by direct competitors, and this
shape of the literature must be explicitly addressed in the M2
deliverable rather than concealed by artificial padding of
references.

The five tradeoff axes specified in the assignment — precision
versus runtime overhead, response time versus schedulability,
optimality versus feasibility, offline versus online operation,
and formal guarantees versus practical deployability — form the
core analytical contribution of M2 and should be applied
systematically to Priority Exchange in comparison with Polling
Server, Deferrable Server, and Sporadic Server. The preliminary
characterisations provided in this interaction will be revised
on the basis of primary-source evidence drawn from Sprunt, Sha
and Lehoczky 1989 and from Buttazzo "Hard Real-Time Computing
Systems".

All bibliographic references, certification-standard claims, and
quantitative aspects of the planning suggestions will be verified
against primary sources prior to incorporation in the submitted
deliverable. The planning artefact is treated as scaffolding for
the contextualisation work and not as a substitute for the
underlying scientific analysis.

entries.ai_output_summary:
Provided a tiered list of verified, freely accessible sources for
Day 1 of the Milestone 2 working plan, organised by primary status
and depth of treatment, with explicit section-level reading
guidance for each item.

Tier 1 — Essential primary sources:
- Sprunt, Sha and Lehoczky 1989, accessed as the Carnegie Mellon
  Software Engineering Institute technical report version
  CMU/SEI-89-TR-11. Reading guidance directed to the abstract and
  introduction for motivation, Section 2 for the background on
  Polling Server and Deferrable Server, Section 3 for the
  Sporadic Server algorithm and its improvement over Priority
  Exchange, Section 4 for the simulation-based performance
  comparison, Section 5 for the schedulability analysis, and the
  reference list for the citation of the Lehoczky, Sha and
  Strosnider 1987 paper on Deferrable Server.
- Spuri and Buttazzo 1994, accessed via the personal RETIS
  laboratory page of Professor Buttazzo. Reading guidance
  directed to the abstract and introduction for the
  positioning of the Earliest Deadline First branch of the
  family tree, Section 2 for the background and confirmation of
  the lineage running through Lehoczky 1987 and Sprunt 1989,
  Section 3 for Dynamic Priority Exchange and Dynamic Sporadic
  Server as Earliest Deadline First analogues of Priority
  Exchange and Sporadic Server, Section 4 for the Total
  Bandwidth Server, and the conclusion for the performance
  comparison.

Tier 2 — Foundation reference:
- Liu and Layland 1973, recommended for citation as the foundation
  of fixed-priority scheduling. Reading guidance limited to the
  abstract and the first two pages for confirmation of the Rate
  Monotonic optimality bound, with the observation that this
  reference is already in use in the Milestone 1 deliverable.

Tier 3 — Lecture-slide summaries used as backup material:
- Real-Time Systems Lecture 6 by Wassim Ahmad, for a concise
  comparison of Polling Server, Deferrable Server, Priority
  Exchange and Sporadic Server.
- CIS 541 course material from the University of Pennsylvania
  by Insup Lee, for worst-case scenarios and timing diagrams
  for Polling Server, Deferrable Server, and Priority Exchange.
- CPEN432 Task Servers slides from the University of British
  Columbia, with explicit slide-range guidance for Polling
  Server, Deferrable Server, Sporadic Server, and Constant
  Bandwidth Server.

Tier 4 — Additional primary source for the most modern algorithm:
- Abeni and Buttazzo 1998 on the Constant Bandwidth Server,
  suggested for retrieval via Google Scholar, with the note
  that the Sprunt 1989 paper does not cover Constant Bandwidth
  Server because it postdates Sprunt by nearly a decade.

A two-hour reading plan was provided in five phases (30 minutes
on the Sprunt paper, 20 minutes on the Spuri and Buttazzo paper,
20 minutes on the CPEN432 slides for Constant Bandwidth Server,
30 minutes of structured note-taking, and 20 minutes of
family-tree sketching). A handwritten template for the resulting
family tree was provided, organised on a horizontal time axis
from 1973 to 1998 and split into a Rate Monotonic branch
(Liu and Layland 1973, Lehoczky, Sha and Strosnider 1987,
Sprunt, Sha and Lehoczky 1989 introducing Priority Exchange and
Sporadic Server) and an Earliest Deadline First branch
(Spuri and Buttazzo 1994 introducing Dynamic Priority Exchange,
Dynamic Sporadic Server, and Total Bandwidth Server, followed by
Abeni and Buttazzo 1998 introducing Constant Bandwidth Server).
A methodological note was included clarifying that the purpose
of the reading is positioning rather than mastery, and that five
extraction facts per algorithm (name, year, authors, improvement
over predecessor, key mechanism in one sentence) are sufficient
for the Milestone 2 deliverable.

actions: The accessibility of each suggested source was verified by web
search prior to inclusion in the recommendation. The Carnegie
Mellon Software Engineering Institute technical report version
of the Sprunt, Sha and Lehoczky 1989 paper was confirmed to be
freely hosted by Carnegie Mellon University and to contain the
same scientific content as the journal version. The Spuri and
Buttazzo 1994 paper was confirmed to be hosted on the personal
RETIS laboratory page of Professor Buttazzo, which is the
canonical legitimate distribution channel for that paper. The
section-level reading guidance for each source was cross-checked
against the standard structure of these papers and against
secondary treatments in Buttazzo "Hard Real-Time Computing
Systems". The lecture-slide sources were verified to be hosted
on institutional domains (Syrian Private University, University
of Pennsylvania, University of British Columbia) consistent with
legitimate academic distribution.

issues: - Direct links to the Liu and Layland 1973 paper and the Abeni
and Buttazzo 1998 paper were not provided; the user is
directed to a search-engine query rather than a verified
hosted location, which introduces an additional step.
- The reading-time estimates (30 minutes for the Sprunt paper,
20 minutes for the Spuri and Buttazzo paper, 20 minutes for
the CPEN432 slides) are indicative and based on the depth
required for the Milestone 2 family-tree extraction; actual
reading time may vary substantially depending on familiarity
with the underlying scheduling theory.
- Section numbers for the Sprunt 1989 paper are stated by name
but page ranges are given only approximately; the user must
verify the section structure against the actual PDF.
- The Wassim Ahmad lecture material is hosted on a Syrian
Private University domain; the institutional provenance was
not deeply verified and the material should be treated as a
pedagogical aid rather than as a citable primary source.
- The CPEN432 slides are course material rather than a peer
reviewed publication; they are appropriate for orientation
but should not be cited in lieu of the primary papers (in
particular Abeni and Buttazzo 1998 for the Constant Bandwidth
Server).
- The handwritten family-tree template uses a simplified
branching structure that abstracts away parallel research
threads (for example, Slack Stealing by Lehoczky and
Ramos-Thuel 1992, and Dual-Priority Scheduling by Davis and
Wellings 1995); these will need to be added in the Competing
Solution Strategies section of the Milestone 2 deliverable.
- The methodological recommendation to limit each algorithm to
five extraction facts is a working heuristic for the
Milestone 2 timeframe; deeper analysis may be required for
the Tradeoff Analysis section.

entries.reflection:
The interaction provided a structured starting point for the
literature-gathering phase of Milestone 2 by identifying verified,
freely accessible versions of the canonical primary sources for
the Priority Exchange algorithm and its surrounding family of
aperiodic server algorithms. The most valuable output is the
identification of the Carnegie Mellon Software Engineering
Institute technical report version of the Sprunt, Sha and
Lehoczky 1989 paper as a freely available primary source, which
removes a common access barrier for the canonical reference on
Priority Exchange. The identification of the Spuri and Buttazzo
1994 paper on the personal RETIS laboratory page of Professor
Buttazzo similarly provides direct access to the Earliest
Deadline First branch of the family tree without recourse to
restricted-access journal databases.

The section-level reading guidance provided for each primary
source allows the Milestone 2 work to proceed in a time-boxed
manner consistent with the available preparation window. The
suggested two-hour structure for the first working session
(reading, note-taking, and family-tree sketching) is a working
plan that will be revised on contact with the actual reading
material; in particular, the depth required for the schedulability
analysis sections of the Sprunt paper may exceed the time
allocation given here.

A residual concern is that the lecture-slide sources, although
useful as orientation material, are not substitutes for the
primary papers and must not be cited in their place in the
Milestone 2 deliverable. The bibliography of Milestone 2 will
draw exclusively from peer reviewed primary sources and from
the textbook reference by Buttazzo, in line with the assignment
specification by Prof. Dr. Henkler and the standard practice
of the seminar.

All bibliographic references and access links will be verified
against their stated hosting locations prior to inclusion in
the final deliverable. Section numbers, author attributions,
and publication years cited from the assistant's output will be
cross-checked against the actual contents of the retrieved
documents. The output of this interaction is treated as a
working source list and not as a substitute for direct
verification of each primary source.
